utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours, counsel and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution Stefan Waespi and Daryl Mundis assisted today by Mr. Andres Vatter our case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. On behalf of Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, lead counsel, Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel, and Alexis Demirdjian, legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On this day the 22nd of March, 2005, I bid good afternoon to all those present, the two representatives of the Prosecution, the six Defence counsel, General Hadzihasanovic, General Kubura, and all those present in this courtroom on the 200th day of hearings. We shall first of all go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed in open session, and we're going to address the question of scheduling for the future weeks and months. So I shall give the floor to the Defence first. Mr. Bourgon, who is already on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We -- before we begin the discussion on the schedule, I would prefer to make a statement in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As we are in open session, the aim of this part of the hearing is to discuss the schedule for the weeks and months ahead, and the Defence told us that they wish to make some observations about this, and Mr. Dixon has asked for some time to be reserved for him, and the Prosecution also needs to provide us with some information. So everyone will have a chance to comment on this issue, but before giving the floor to the parties, I wish to recall that we, the Judges, also have scheduling constraints. As you know, due to the judicial -- the court holidays or the court recess which begins in the week of the 24th of July, so we can't go beyond that. And also the Judges are having a Plenary meeting on the 21st of July. So in any event, should it be necessary, the last hearing can be held on the 20th of July and not after that. So the 20th July is the limit, the extreme limit. So this should be borne in mind. We've also noted that there is a week that will -- when we will not be sitting. That is the week from the 25th to the 29th of April, the 29th being a UN holiday. Consequently, we have the end of the month of March, the three weeks in April, the four weeks of May, four weeks in June, and three first weeks of July on the outside. So within that time period, everything has to be completed. Who wishes to take the floor first? Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Perhaps it's best if I commence and then Mr. Mundis can follow me. Your Honours, if I can say on behalf of all the parties having met each other, we are confident that we can finish everything within the time period that Your Honours have outlined and hopefully can be done sooner than that. Your Honours, looking at the case for Mr. Kubura, we propose that his case should commence on the 11th of April. The reason why I gave that date, Your Honour, is that if we do finish the military expert by Friday the 1st of April, we would request a one-week break in the week commencing 4 April before we start our case. We wish to use that week to make final contact with our witnesses and to bring many of them or make arrangements to bring them to The Hague so that they can be ready to testify thereafter. There will also be matters that we need to sort out with the Prosecution in terms of documents and finalising any matters relating to translation as well. I can report on that matter, Your Honour, that at this stage we foresee no problems with relation to the translation of the documents we propose to use. We were initially granted six weeks by Your Honours for our case. We will be able to do our case within five weeks, and we therefore use -- wish to use the additional week as the week for the break before the start of our case, the week commencing 4 April, and then to take five weeks thereafter to complete our case taking into account the breaks in the week Your Honour mentioned commencing 25 April, to finish our case by the week ending 20 May. Your Honours, I will talk more about how we will present the case for Mr. Kubura, but before I do that, I did just wish to comment on the closure of the case for Mr. Hadzihasanovic on the 1st of April. We are using that date on the assumption that the expert witness can be completed by then and also that any other matters such as Rule 92 bis matters will also be finalised by then. If that wasn't to be the case, of course the agenda would then have to shift back, and we would request that no matter when the team for Mr. Hadzihasanovic closes its case, we are given the opportunity to have a one-week break before we commence our case. If, as Mr. Bourgon said yesterday, he's able to complete his examination-in-chief of the military expert by the end of this week, we would require no more than two hours on Tuesday with the military expert, and as Mr. Mundis has said yesterday as well, he would require approximately a day and a half, which would mean that by approximately Wednesday next week, the cross-examination is complete, leaving some time thereafter the Thursday and the Friday for re-examination and questions by Your Honours. That would mean that we can finish everything by the 1st of April, subject of course to any other outstanding matters that might arise. In addition to that through the helpful inquiries of the registrar, we have been able to ascertain that there would be the possibility of having additional hearings next week. I see Mr. Registrar is shaking his head. But the last indication were is we would have the possibility of adding if necessary, let's hope it doesn't come to that, but if necessary we could use extra time next week to finish by 1 April. If that is not possible, Your Honours, then we are going to have to ensure that we use the time available to finish by 1 April. If it goes over 1 April, our only request is that we still be given a week when the Hadzihasanovic team closes its case before we start our case, whenever that might be. So that is our first request, Your Honour. In respect of the way in which the case for Mr. Kubura will be presented, assuming that we then commence with the opening on the 11th of April, we would request that we only schedule witnesses for four days per week, from Monday until Thursday, and that we do not schedule any witnesses for the Friday of each week on the basis that we can use the Friday as a reserve day if we run over, but more importantly that we can use that day to finalise with the Prosecution any documents that we are going to present to witnesses the following week, make sure all translations are in order, and also provide further information in respect of our Rule 65 summaries if necessary. That would over a five-week period give us approximately 20 days of court time, that's excluding the Fridays of each week, and we have assessed that we could complete all of our witnesses within that time. We will have approximately 20 witnesses. A final list is being prepared and will be forwarded to Your Honours and the Prosecution by the end of this month. As Your Honours will recall, the list we had initially was a provisional list and we were given the option of putting in a final list before we commenced our case. So we would be looking at approximately one witness per day, sitting four days a week with the Friday off for preparation but there to use if we need it, if there is any running over of time. So that is our second request, Your Honour, that we are permitted to schedule witnesses for four days of the week only. And we have worked out that we would be able to then complete our case by Friday, the 20th of May. Your Honour, the witnesses that are to be called are mostly witnesses who were members of the 7th Brigade at the time. We will not be calling any witnesses as to questions of general context. The witnesses will all focus on the key allegations made against Mr. Kubura and, amongst other things, will focus on showing that the 7th Brigade was not involved in any of the alleged offences that are put forward in the indictment. In respect of those witnesses, there are two former members of the 7th Brigade who are currently serving with the UN in UN missions outside of Bosnia, and we are making arrangements to make sure they are able to come here during the five-week period that we present our case. We might, therefore, have to be a little flexible in terms of when they appear because they need to get permission from the United Nations to come here to testify. We don't anticipate there will be any problems with them coming, but we just need to be able to fit them in when exactly they are able to get leave in that five-week period. And the second matter is that we will in all likelihood make an application for two persons to give testimony by videolink because of their health condition. I have not yet had the opportunity to speak to Mr. Mundis about this issue, but I will do so in due course, and it might be possible that this can be resolved between us so that a joint application is made to Your Honours for that videolink to be set up at a time that is convenient for both of the parties, once again during the five-week period that I have identified. As I've also said, we do not anticipate at this stage that there will be any translation problems of the documents that we do wish to show the witnesses. A list has already been prepared and those documents have been given to the Prosecution, and many of those documents will be used by the witnesses who do attend. So, Your Honours, at this stage I merely bring to your attention that the only two potential areas where the schedule might be disrupted is the witnesses coming from the UN and the videolink, but we don't anticipate that that would change the five-week period that we will use for our case. Your Honour, those are our submissions in respect of how we propose to present the case for Mr. Kubura, and assuming that the team for Mr. Hadzihasanovic completes by 1 April, that would be the schedule that we propose, a one-week break, then commencing on the 11th of April, running for two weeks, having a further week break as Your Honours have indicated, and then a final three weeks, closing by Friday, the 20th of May. Your Honour, our applications would be that if that is in order with you that that be granted so that we can then commence our planning to ensure that the witnesses are brought here in time. Thank you for the opportunity to address that matter. I know my learned friend Mr. Mundis has submissions to make in response. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this information. The Judges will discuss the matter, but I would personally like to say that what you have suggested seems quite acceptable to me. The two outstanding problems concern the two witnesses who work for the UN. Naturally you should soon take the necessary steps to obtain authorisation for them appear as witnesses. And then, as you know, the videolink is a means that we have accepted, but this depends on the medical condition of witnesses. I assume that you have medical arguments in support of your request. This could proceed very quickly because the registrar has all the resources necessary. So we have 20 witnesses who are to appear at 20 hearings, and if everything goes as we hope, the case should be closed -- your case should be closed by the 20th of May provided that we can start with your case on the 11th of April. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm sure it was a slight oversight by my learned colleague, Mr. Dixon, but when the parties first met several weeks ago at my invitation, we all agreed and wanted to reiterate that of course all issues pertaining to the scheduling is at the control or under the control of the Trial Chamber and what the parties were seeking to do first by meeting together and then by meeting with the Chamber's legal officer and senior legal officer was to attempt to come up with some scheduling ideas that were me actually agreeable to the parties in order to put that before Your Honours with the hopeful expectation that what we had proposed would be acceptable. But of course we all understand that scheduling and control of the proceedings is fully in the hands of the Trial Chamber. Let me just respond to what distinct issues with respect to the completion of the Hadzihasanovic case. As my learned colleague Mr. Dixon pointed out, I did inform the Defence for both teams as well as the Chamber's legal officer that based on the completion of our analysis of the expert's report, it is anticipated that the Prosecution will require no more than a day and a half to conduct its cross-examination. That of course is subject to the caveat that we haven't heard all of the witness's testimony, so I may need additional -- a little bit more time in the event that during his viva voce testimony he expands upon some of the areas covered in his report. Nevertheless, assuming again that Mr. Bourgon completes his direct examination by the end of this week and that the Kubura team takes two hours, I would expect to be done with the cross-examination by the completion of our session on Wednesday, allowing two days, Thursday and Friday, for re-examination and any questions that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the Bench may have following examination by the parties. So I don't anticipate the need for any additional sittings next week in order to complete the testimony of the expert witness. The second issue concerning the Hadzihasanovic -- completion of the Hadzihasanovic case relates to the proposed 92 bis witness statements. Your Honours are aware that the parties are in the process of discussing that. We have informed the Hadzihasanovic Defence team that, of the proposed witness statements, we're still reviewing two of them, but with respect to the remainder of those, the Prosecution will not object to those. I'm putting that on the record. Nor will we seek to have those witnesses brought here for purposes of cross-examination. I expect to have our analysis of the final two statements done within the next day or so and I'll inform the Defence of that accordingly, but we don't anticipate any problems with respect to the proposed written witness statements that the Hadzihasanovic Defence has or will be filing before Your Honours. So we don't anticipate any problems with either the expert or the 92 bis statements in terms of impacting on the ability of the Hadzihasanovic team to finish their trial by the 1st of April. With respect to all of the scheduling issues raised by my learned friend from the Kubura Defence, the Prosecution certainly agrees with their proposals and thinks that their proposed schedule is both a reasonable one and one which will allow us to complete the Kubura Defence case by the 20th of May. I wouldn't anticipate any problems with the videolink testimony, of course pending proper medical reports with respect to the two witnesses that they've proposed to be heard by way of videolink. That brings me, Mr. President and Your Honours, to the first topic that concerns the Prosecution, and that is, as Your Honours can probably anticipate, the Prosecution will be filing a motion seeking leave to reopen our case with respect to tendering a number of documents. I stress the documents, because at this point, and we are finalising our consideration on this issue, I wouldn't expect that we would be seeking leave to call witnesses, although it's possible there may be a small number of witnesses that we might seek leave to have called, and this of course can also depend upon the position taken by the two Defence teams, as Your Honours undoubtedly will recall during the Prosecution case when large numbers of documents were tendered from the bar table the Defence suggested that we have witnesses come in and testify about the documents, where they came from, et cetera. So if the Chamber wishes us to call people from the archives or investigators who receive the documents or investigators who seize the documents, we may seek leave to do that, or of course if ordered to do so, we will endeavour to bring those witnesses. With respect to the documents, Mr. President, we anticipate that we're talking less than 50 documents. All of the documents have previously been disclosed -- as of this date have been disclosed to the Defence. Once we have identified the precise documents that we will be filing a motion seeking leave to reopen, we will then disclose those specific documents to both Defence teams so there is no confusion as to which documents are being considered. We are working and endeavouring to file this motion as quickly as possible so that the Defence can have an opportunity to respond to that filing and, in the event that the Prosecution is granted lever to reopen, we would seek the Trial Chamber's permission to do that immediately after the close of the Kubura case. That would be the week commencing the 23rd of May, so that there is no interruption or long gaps where time is being eaten up pending resolution of the issue of the Prosecution reopening of its case. So our goal is to get this motion filed as quickly as possible so that the responses can be filed and Your Honours will have time to consider our application to reopen our case, and if that is granted in total or in part, we could immediately do that during the week of the 23rd of May. And of course if the Defence requires additional time in order to reopen parts of their case, that is entirely up to them, but we'll have to just basically see how it goes with respect to the Prosecution motion to reopen. With respect to scheduling I do have one other issue, Mr. President, that I would ask to address the Chamber in private session if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're back in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'd just like to make a few comments with regard to the Prosecution's request to open their case. If I have understood the Prosecution, they want to reopen their case. It's not a matter of rebuttal evidence. Mr. President, for the Defence it's important that the procedure followed, that is to say whether or not the Prosecution be allowed to reopen their case, this is something that should be determined on an objective basis and above all we must be familiar with the procedures followed. There are certain conditions that must be met, Mr. President in order to be granted leave to reopen one's case. This does not necessarily depend on the content of the evidence one wants to presents but, rather, on the reason for which the Prosecution feels it is necessary to present additional evidence to its case and the reasons for which they should be granted leave to do so. Mr. President, this is why we suggest a twofold procedure should be followed. First of all, the Prosecution -- we would like the Prosecution to inform us in its motion of the reasons for which they would like to be granted leave to reopen their case. We'd also like to be informed of the justification for such a course of action. We'd also like to be informed of when the documents would be disclosed to us and in particular to know whether these documents have already been disclosed to us. If these are documents that have already been disclosed then we have no problem. It is sufficient to inform us of the exhibit numbers. And also we would like to know in what manner these documents will be taken into consideration. We believe that a decision should first be rendered with regard to how opportune it is to reopen their case, and then we should be provided with information of the assessment of the evidence. We believe that there are two stages that have to be followed. First of all, there should be a request for leave to be granted, a motion for leave to be granted, then we should have an assessment of what the Prosecution actually desires in terms of witnesses and documents. When I have a look at the dates that the Prosecution has put forward, naturally at this point in time we don't know what the Trial Chamber has in mind in terms of -- or in regard to additional evidence. We don't know whether there will be additional evidence or not. But we have in such a case very little time left for the closing arguments in July. We believe that the schedule might be somewhat overcharged depending on what the Chamber desires as far as additional evidence is concerned, whether this evidence takes the forms of witnesses or documents. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we could perhaps go into private session for the responses.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in open session I'm asking the Prosecution to tell me what the legal basis is for the request to reopen the Prosecution case, and I wanted to know whether it was based on Rule 85 paragraph (A)(iii), or on the jurisprudence of the Tribunal with respect to the reopening of a case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. It is in respect of the jurisprudence of the Tribunal. Rule -- our interpretation of Rule 85(A)(iii) is that that type of evidence pursuant to the Rule which refers to rebuttal would be the type of evidence which the Prosecution could not have reasonably anticipated putting before the Trial Chamber during the Prosecution case in chief. We are talking here about evidence which came into our possession after the close of our case. Therefore, we couldn't have anticipated making such evidence available to Your Honours. Your Honours might recall previously the Trial Chamber actually referred the parties to the Celebici appeals judgement which talks about reopening. We will be relying on and our motion will put forward our position, but we are relying on the jurisprudence of the Tribunal and case law to the effect of the legal standards that are involved in reopening of a case, particularly when one is dealing with evidence that came into one of the party's possession after the close of their case. So we're not at this point talking about a case in rebuttal but, rather, reopening our case with respect to evidence which came into our possession after the close of our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Does the Defence have anything to add? Mr. Bourgon? No? The other Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you, yes. I know this matter will be discussed at length in the motions, but if we can at this point simply clarify that, as my learned friend has said, all of the documents that they will be relying upon they weren't in receipt of before they closed their case, and that they will only be seeking to introduce documents which they actually received after the close of the case. I think that narrows the issue much more, because we have seen documents presented in cross-examination that the Prosecution did have before the close of their case which were disclosed to us but which they didn't choose to introduce in their case, and there have been instances where some of those documents have been introduced for the limited purpose of memory refreshing. And as I understand from what my learned friend is saying, none of those documents will be applied to be introduced after the close of their case but it is only documents they received after the -- the close of their case. Our submission will be, Your Honours, and of course we will outline this more once we have the motion, as I said earlier on, that if those documents could have been obtained during the Prosecution case through proper investigation and due diligence, then the Prosecution should not be permitted now when they have obtained the information through ongoing investigations to use that material. If that material was readily available to them in 2000 or 2001, then that's when it should have been obtained, and they should not be permitted to investigating endlessly. As we've said many times before some end has to be put to this matter. But we will outline that more in our written submissions and oral submissions later, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me -- let me again stress so that everyone is 100 per cent absolutely clear. I have directed the members of our trial team and the support team for this members of this trial team to consider only documents that came into the Prosecution's possession after the close of our case. We are not considering any documents that we had in our possession prior to the close of our case. The issue of due diligence will be addressed in our -- in our motion but just so that everyone is clear, we are only focusing on documents that came into our possession after the 22nd of July, 2004, which, if memory serves me, is the day the Prosecution rested its case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Looking at the transcript in English, Mr. Dixon son has contributed a small shade of meaning. They are telling us that the Prosecution should not be granted leave to produce new documents if they had the ability to have them before in the year 2000 and 2001. This is a very fine nuance. What is the position of the Prosecution regarding this point?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, without going into too great of detail, the case law does require the Prosecution or any party seeking to reopen its case or to present additional evidence such as additional evidence on appeal pursuant to Rule 115 and the standards are -- are very, very similar, the party who wishes to put additional or new evidence before a Chamber must demonstrate due diligence. Our motion will -- will address the issue of due diligence and the steps that were taken in terms of the investigation of this case. We will do that by attaching to our motion some of the requests what we call requests for assistance, RFAs, which are documents that we send to the Bosnian authorities seeking access to archives, documents, et cetera, witnesses. We will attach some of those requests for assistance to our motion as annexes demonstrating the steps we took. I also anticipate that attached to our motion there very well might be an affidavit from the deputy investigation commander who oversaw, among other things, the investigation of this case, who will explain in his affidavit or statement the steps that were taken with respect to some of the archives. But let me also say that which again should not come as a surprise, as the Trial Chamber is aware, the Tribunal -- or the Prosecution and the Tribunal earlier this year has indicted Rasim Delic, and many of the investigative steps that resulted in us obtaining these documents after the close of the Prosecution case against the two accused in this courtroom, these documents were obtained pursuant to our investigation which resulted in the indictment of Rasim Delic. So what happened was we were looking at a different time period, that is 1995, and among the material pertaining to 1995 were documents relating to 1993, for example. And so our motion will set forth exactly what steps we took, what access we had to certain archives, and the results of those steps which, our view is, will explain the steps we took with respect to this investigation and our submission in our written pleadings will explain fully what steps were taken and what the results of those steps were, whether access was granted or whether access for whatever reason was denied to us to go in and search certain archives for material. But we will -- I anticipate our motion will be very clear as to the steps we took. We will be explaining basically the source of the documents. They come from one of three archives as well as a specific request for assistance concerning court records of Mr. Ramo Durmis, which is a fourth category. Our motion will be -- will break down the documents in terms of where they came from and will explain to the Trial Chamber the steps that we took in fulfilling the due diligence obligations that we have. So we believe that our motion will address these issues, and of course the Defence will respond to our motion and -- so that the Trial Chamber is in a position to render whatever decision the Chamber feels best advances the cause of truth finding and justice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The sooner the better. So please seek to file those motions as soon as possible so that the Defence can respond and so that we, too, will be able to render our decisions in writing so as to avoid any waste of time. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We are having an exchange of view about the investigations, but the point that I wish to address is that the decision on granting leave should be separate from the decision on the substance. What I wish to say is that the documents should be mixed with the decision to reopen or not. When the Prosecution presents its arguments about due diligence in obtaining those documents, we believe that it is important not to consider the documents at that stage but, rather, to consider how certain documents were obtained, and then if a grant -- leave is granted, then we can look at the substance of those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Mundis, the Defence would like your motion to be divided up into two. First, motion to seek leave to reopen and then the motion will be motivated by the fact that you did not have knowledge of those documents, that you discovered them during subsequent investigations, et cetera. And once the decision is rendered regarding the opportuneness of reopening the case, then there would be a second motion regarding the admission of so many documents, which would allow the Defence the possibility to challenge the documents one by one. So they are suggesting that you divide this procedure into two.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Which again, Mr. President, is -- comes as no surprise. The Defence informed us of their position with respect to this question of modalities during our earlier meetings. Our position, Mr. President, really is a twofold one. First of all, the proposed procedure that Mr. Bourgon has described would inevitably take many, many weeks to complete in terms of us filing a motions, the Defence responding, a written response from the Chamber, then us filing a second motion, then the Defence responding, then perhaps a document-by-document argument similar to the contested document hearings we had during the course of the trial followed by a decision, followed by us reopening, tendering the documents, and closing our case. Our position is that the Tribunal is comprised of Trial Chambers made up of professional Judges. There can be, and I've said this in other contexts, there can be no prejudice with professional Judges, and so our position is: In order to expedite the proceedings, there is no need to go through a two-step process because the two-step process will inevitably mean that we do not finish our work here by the 20th of July or, alternatively, because of the length of time involved, the Prosecution is precluded from putting important new evidence before Your Honours, thus precluding perhaps the Trial Chamber from completely fulfilling its duties and responsibilities. Our view is because Your Honours are professional Judges and because the issue of prejudice does not arise when we're dealing with professional Judges, we believe the best course of action would be for Your Honours to have our motion, have any documents that explain the due diligence steps that we take attached as annexes and for us to file at the same time the proposed documents so that Your Honours can make determinations as to the relevance or importance of the documents all in one decision-making process, if you will. We believe that the alternative would be a timely one and because of the fact that Your Honours are professional Judges, we believe that the issue of potential prejudice is -- is, to use a colloquial term, a non-starter because of the nature of cases held and heard before Trial Chambers of professional Judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to remind the parties that when they file a motion they do what they wish, and then it's up to the Judges to appreciate and assess them. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I haven't counted the number of times the word "professional" was used, but in any way, we are fully aware that the Chamber is highly professional, and this is something that the Defence has never doubted. That is not the point. The point is that when we're talking about due diligence in obtaining something is one thing, and what is the content of the document is quite a different matter. These are two separate matters. I wanted to get a document. Did I show due diligence in obtaining it? That is one thing. What is the document and what is its use is another matter. This document should not be an argument to affect the due diligence discussion, and we believe that there is every possibility of completing everything within the time limits discussed. The Prosecution file their motion, then we respond very quickly to expedite things. If leave is granted, if it has fulfilled the criteria necessary for reopening, then we look at the documents. I think it is the week of the 3rd of May. We will have plenty of time to see during that week, to see what the documents are, by the point is whether the Prosecution fulfils the criteria to be granted leave to reopen its case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will discuss this amongst ourselves, and we will let you know what is to be done. I should like us to go into private session once again.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now that we are in open session, are there any other matters to be raised? If there are no other matters to be raised, I invite you to come to the hearing that will start tomorrow at 2.15. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
